analysis.one_liner: Lets student loan borrowers refinance at lower rates, paid for by a 30% minimum tax on income over $1 million.
analysis.headline: Introduced in March 2019 with 35 cosponsors, the bill never received a committee hearing or vote and died when the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let people with older federal student loans, and borrowers current on private student loans, swap them for new federal loans at the lower fixed interest rates new borrowers got in the 2016-17 school year. It directs the Education Department to prioritize borrowers with the most financial need, and it is paid for by a new minimum tax requiring taxpayers earning over $1 million to pay at least 30% of that income. The refinancing window would close after two years or once its cost equals the new tax revenue.
analysis.who_benefits: Student loan borrowers, especially those with older loans at higher interest rates and those the Education Department deems most in financial need. Federal borrowers with loans issued before July 2019 could refinance down to 2016-17 rates, and borrowers current on private student loans could move those loans into the federal system at federal rates with federal borrower protections. Borrowers who refinance would keep their repayment timelines and their progress toward income-based repayment.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Student loan borrowers with high-rate loans

how_it_helps.text: Allows qualified borrowers with federal loans issued before July 2019, including older bank-based FFEL loans, to refinance at the fixed 2016-17 federal student loan rates.
Creates a federal program to buy out qualifying private student loans and reissue them as federal loans at 2016-17 rates, replacing the private lender as the holder of the debt.

Directs the Education Department to write eligibility rules based on income or debt-to-income ratio that prioritize borrowers with the greatest financial need, and to run a campaign notifying borrowers they can apply.
Preserves repayment credit: payments made on the original federal loan count toward income-based repayment forgiveness and public service loan forgiveness timelines after refinancing.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers with adjusted gross income over $1 million, who would face a 30% minimum tax on income above roughly a charitable-deduction-adjusted threshold, indexed to inflation. Private student lenders would also give up loans and interest income when the government pays off their loans at par.
analysis.who_pays_short: Households earning over $1 million a year

drawbacks.text: The refinancing program is temporary: it must terminate two years after enactment, or sooner if its cost equals the revenue from the new tax.

Refinanced private loans would not qualify for public service loan forgiveness, teacher loan repayment programs, or credit for payments made before refinancing, and borrowers must have been current for six months — people already in default are excluded.
The 30% minimum tax is a substantial permanent tax increase on high-income households, which opponents argued would reduce investment and job growth.
Relief is a one-time interest-rate reset for existing borrowers; it does nothing for future students facing high tuition or new debt.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For borrowers locked into 6-8% loans from the 2000s, refinancing to roughly 3-5% rates would have saved meaningful money over the life of the loans, and the bill was designed to be deficit-neutral by pairing those savings with a tax on a small slice of top earners. The honest costs are real: a permanent new minimum tax on high incomes to fund a two-year, one-time refinancing window, and a carve-out that leaves defaulted borrowers and some forgiveness prospects outside the program. The design tradeoffs are debatable, but the bill never got far enough for the tradeoff to be argued on the floor.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Finance Committee received the bill and never acted on it; it died at the end of the 116th Congress with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote.

narrative.text: Senator Elizabeth Warren introduced the bill on March 13, 2019, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the same day.
Thirty-five senators cosponsored the bill — 34 Democrats and 1 independent — including most of the Democratic conference and Joe Manchin, but no Republicans.
The action history shows no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action, and no roll call of any kind after the referral; the bill expired when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Borrowers with high-rate student loans keep paying their original interest rates. Households earning over $1 million avoid the 30% minimum tax, and private student lenders keep their loan books and interest income — the bill's intended payfors never took effect.

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 35 Senate cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on March 13, 2019 and took no recorded action for the rest of the Congress — no hearing or markup was ever scheduled.

against.name: Sen. Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: As chairman of the committee of referral, never scheduled the bill for consideration.

against.name: Sen. Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Did not bring the bill to the Senate floor; the Senate majority did not schedule floor time for Warren's student debt bills in the 116th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 36 sponsors were Democrats or the chamber's independent (Bernie Sanders); not a single Republican cosponsored, and the bill never advanced in the Republican-run Senate.

industries.note: The bill would have let the Education Department pay off qualifying private student loans at par and reissue them as cheaper federal loans, moving those balances and future interest income out of private lenders' hands. Borrowers current on their loans would gain federal rates and protections the private market does not offer.
A new 30% minimum tax on income above $1 million (adjusted for a charitable deduction and inflation) would raise these households' effective tax rate permanently to fund the refinancing program.

Refinancing would swap some high-rate loans for lower-rate ones, trimming interest-driven revenue, but the bill requires servicers to notify borrowers about their refinancing eligibility and the loans would remain serviced under federal programs.
